subject: Factors in sqldf files created by read.csv.sql

messages.author: 87e100fbbe32313a
messages.subject: Factors in sqldf files created by read.csv.sql
parts:
I am trying to figure out how to create an SQLite database containing roughly 30 gig of data from the Census's Current Population Survey (CPS) in a form where I can get the data back out without having to do complicated joins on with multi-gig files that create memory problems. I know that this is not what sqldf was created for, but it does seem to be set up to understand R data types. This is crucial for my application, as most of the columns -- over 300 of them -- are factors.

If I am understanding the documentation correctly, columns in sqldf objects normally take their data class and factor levels from the data frames they are read from, and pass that information back to R with any data extracted from the sqldf object. My question is, if I read the data in using read.csv.sql, to avoid the R memory bottleneck, is there an alternate way to inform the sqldf file what the data types and factor levels are?

Finally, if I am reading multiple files into a single sqldf object, will I have difficulty if some columns have the same names and some do not? And specifically, can I assign data types to just the new columns, and expect that the shared columns will take their data type from the previous assignment, or would that lead to the kind of the conflicts that disable column class as described in FAQ section #1.

Any help or pointers would be much appreciated.

Sincerely, Andrew

On Tuesday, October 1, 2013 3:27:36 PM UTC-4, Andrew Hoerner wrote:
I am trying to figure out how to create an SQLite database containing  roughly 30 gig of data from the Census's Current Population Survey (CPS) in a form where I can get the data back out without having to do complicated joins on with multi-gig files that create memory problems. I know that this is not what sqldf was created for, but it does seem to be set up to understand R data types. This is crucial for my application, as most of the columns -- over 300 of them -- are factors.

If I am understanding the documentation correctly, columns in sqldf objects normally take their data class and factor levels from the data frames they are read from, and pass that information back to R with any data extracted from the sqldf object. My question is, if I read the data in using read.csv.sql, to avoid the R memory bottleneck, is there an alternate way to inform the sqldf file what the data types and factor levels are?

Finally, if I am reading multiple files into a single sqldf object, will I have difficulty if some columns have the same names and some do not? And specifically, can I assign data types to just the new columns, and expect that the shared columns will take their data type from the previous assignment, or would that lead to the kind of the conflicts that disable column class as described in FAQ section #1

read.csv.sql is just a thin wrapper around sqldf.  It sets up the arguments appropriately so what applies to sqldf mostly applies to read.csv.sql too.  The sqldf method= argument determines how classes are assigned to output columns and  is described in ?sqldf .  The default is method = "auto" but you can use other valid values described there and you can also use your own function as described there as well.  Also you could just employ the method = "raw" argument (which uses the classes as they come from RSQLite) and then change the classes of the output yourself.  For example:


    to.factor <- function(DF) {
        is.char <- sapply(DF, is.character)
        replace(DF, is.char, lapply(DF[is.char], factor))
    }

    # 1
    DF <- read.csv.sql("myfile.csv", method = "raw")
    DF <- to.factor(DF)

    # 2 - or equivalently
    DF <- read.csv.sql("myfile.csv", method = to.factor)   

I am not clear on the last question but if you are rbind'ing data frames normally they should have the same names.  There is rbind.fill in the plyr package which can handle cetain situations where the names are not the same.  If you are combining them using sql union then the tables must have the same number of columns and same types.
